record.tranche_reason: The study compares downstream task scores for two sizes of RoBERTa, a different measurement setting from pretraining-loss scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper cites scaling work as background, but cited results are not recorded. The relevant own results are the RoBERTa base-versus-large downstream test scores in Table 8. Other model and benchmark scores do not compare scale and are not rows for these claim versions.
record.test_reason: Appendix E fine-tunes RoBERTa-base (125M) and RoBERTa-large (355M) on seven legal tasks and reports test F1 for both. This is a two-point downstream scale comparison in a new setting, legal fine-tuning, bearing on V6. There are no loss sweeps, fits or allocation results.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors say RoBERTa-large gives 'substantial' gains across all tasks and is comparable to or better than the legal models in some cases. They infer that larger legal-oriented models trained on larger legal corpora should gain. Note that several gains are well under 1 F1 (EUR-LEX, LEDGAR µ-F1, UNFAIR µ-F1), so 'substantial across all tasks' overstates the test numbers.
record.recipe_differences: Fine-tunes two pretrained RoBERTa sizes and compares downstream benchmark scores; it does not measure held-out pretraining loss or fit scaling laws.
record.problems: The scale comparison covers only two RoBERTa sizes and does not test a functional scaling trend or predictability. Table 8 reports selected-run test scores without test-set uncertainty estimates. Development-set results are also reported, but are not extracted here because the flattened table layout does not support confidently assigning all values.
record.rows_left_out: Development-set RoBERTa size-comparison values in Table 8 are omitted because the flattened layout makes assignment to model, task, and metric uncertain.

untested.parts: No shape comparison at fixed parameters.
No power-law form tested in any regime. Fine-tuning is used, but no scaling curve is fitted.
Only two model sizes. No predictive curve, no relation to pretraining loss, and no extrapolation of downstream scores.
No exponents or fitting choices compared.

missing.what: Development-set RoBERTa base vs large scores. As flattened, SCOTUS dev appears reversed (µ-F1 77.5→74.6, m-F1 64.1→56.9), but column alignment is uncertain: Legal-BERT dev SCOTUS/EUR-LEX values conflict with Table 5. Needs checking against the PDF.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is a legal NLU benchmark; scale is a side analysis in Appendix E. For all rows, the comparison has two confounds. The large model was fine-tuned with AdamW, lr 1e-5, warm-up 0.1 and weight decay 0.06, while base used Adam at 3e-5. Each score is a single best-dev-seed result with no test uncertainty. Kaplan et al. is cited only as background.

versions.untested_parts: No sweep of held-out pretraining loss against parameter count, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or extrapolation to larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation comparison or compute-optimal parameter/token trends.
No controlled comparison of depth, width, or architecture at fixed parameter count.
No scaling-law tests in other modalities or training regimes.
The study compares only RoBERTa base and large; it does not test a predictive curve over multiple scales or performance as a function of pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitted exponents, compute-optimal splits, or fitting choices.

relationships.condition: RoBERTa-large vs base, test set: ECtHR A/B, SCOTUS, LEDGAR m-F1, UNFAIR-ToS m-F1, CaseHOLD
relationships.reason: Larger model gains +1.3 to +8.6 F1 on these tasks/metrics (R1–R6, R10, R12, R13). This is a two-point comparison only, with a fine-tuning recipe confound.
relationships.display_finding: The larger model gained 1.3–8.6 F1 across the specified tasks and metrics, although the two-model comparison also differed in fine-tuning recipe.

relationships.condition: RoBERTa-large vs base on EUR-LEX, LEDGAR µ-F1, UNFAIR-ToS µ-F1
relationships.reason: Gains shrink to +0.2 to +0.7, within or near seed noise (R7, R8, R9, R11). So the 2.8× size increase helps little on some tasks.
relationships.display_finding: A 2.8-fold size increase yields gains of only 0.2–0.7 points, within or near variation across random seeds.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.condition: RoBERTa base versus large on the seven LexGLUE test datasets
reader_labels.reason: The larger RoBERTa has higher reported test scores on every listed task and metric (R1–R13); this supports scale-related improvement in this comparison, not a predictive scaling curve.
